title: Assassination of John F. Kennedy
wiki_lead:
On Friday, November 22, 1963, John F. Kennedy, the 35th president of the United States, was assassinated while riding in a presidential motorcade through Dallas, Texas. Kennedy was in the vehicle with First Lady Jacqueline Kennedy, Texas governor John Connally, and Connally's wife Nellie, when he was fatally shot from the nearby Texas School Book Depository by Lee Harvey Oswald, a former U.S. Marine. The motorcade rushed to Parkland Memorial Hospital, where Kennedy was pronounced dead about 30 minutes after the shooting; Connally was also wounded in the attack but recovered. Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson was hastily sworn in as president two hours and eight minutes later aboard Air Force One at Dallas Love Field.
After the assassination, Oswald returned home to retrieve a pistol; he shot and killed a lone Dallas policeman J. D. Tippit shortly afterwards. Around 70 minutes after Kennedy and Connally were shot, Oswald was apprehended by the Dallas Police Department and charged under Texas state law with the murders of Kennedy and Tippit. Two days later, as live television cameras covered Oswald being moved through the basement of Dallas Police Headquarters, he was fatally shot by Dallas nightclub operator Jack Ruby. Like Kennedy, Oswald was taken to Parkland Memorial Hospital, where he soon died. Ruby was convicted of Oswald's murder, though the decision was overturned on appeal, and Ruby died in prison in 1967 while awaiting a new trial.
After a 10-month investigation, the Warren Commission concluded that Oswald assassinated Kennedy, and that there was no evidence that either Oswald or Ruby was part of a conspiracy. In 1967, New Orleans district attorney Jim Garrison brought the only trial for Kennedy's murder against businessman Clay Shaw; Shaw was acquitted. Subsequent federal investigations—such as the Rockefeller Commission and Church Committee—agreed with the Warren Commission's general findings. In its 1979 report, the United States House Select Committee on Assassinations (HSCA) concluded that Kennedy was likely "assassinated as a result of a conspiracy". The HSCA did not identify possible conspirators, but concluded that there was "a high probability that two gunmen fired at [the] President". The HSCA's conclusions were largely based on a police Dictabelt recording, which was subsequently debunked by the U.S. Justice Department.
Kennedy's assassination is still the subject of widespread debate and has spawned many conspiracy theories and alternative scenarios; polls have found that a vast majority of Americans believe there was a conspiracy. The assassination left a profound impact and was the first of four major assassinations during the 1960s in the United States, coming two years before the assassination of Malcolm X in 1965, and five years before the assassinations of Martin Luther King Jr. and Kennedy's brother Robert F. Kennedy in 1968. Kennedy was the fourth U.S. president to be assassinated and is the most recent to have died in office.

grok_lead: The assassination of John F. Kennedy, the 35th President of the United States, took place on November 22, 1963, in Dallas, Texas, when he was struck by bullets fired from a rifle while riding in an open-top limousine through Dealey Plaza during a public motorcade. Kennedy sustained wounds to his upper back and head, the latter proving fatal, and was pronounced dead at Parkland Memorial Hospital approximately 30 minutes after the shooting began at 12:30 p.m. local time. Texas Governor John Connally, seated in front of Kennedy, was also wounded but survived. Lee Harvey Oswald, a former U.S. Marine with pro-Castro sympathies who had defected to the Soviet Union before returning, was identified as the shooter after eyewitnesses placed him at a sixth-floor window of the nearby Texas School Book Depository, from which three shots were fired. Oswald fled the scene, murdered Dallas police officer J.D. Tippit en route, and was arrested about 80 minutes after the assassination on charges including both killings. Two days later, while being transferred in police custody, Oswald was shot and killed on live television by Jack Ruby, a Dallas nightclub owner with underworld ties, precluding a trial that might have clarified his motives or accomplices. President Lyndon B. Johnson established the Warren Commission to investigate, which concluded in 1964 that Oswald acted alone in assassinating Kennedy, firing all shots from the Depository without evidence of conspiracy. The report's single-bullet theory, positing one projectile caused multiple wounds to Kennedy and Connally, has faced scrutiny for anatomical implausibility, while Oswald's brief Soviet residency, Fair Play for Cuba activities, and contacts with intelligence figures raised questions about foreign or domestic involvement overlooked by the Commission. A 1979 House Select Committee on Assassinations review affirmed Oswald fired shots that struck Kennedy and Connally, found a "high probability" that two gunmen fired based on acoustic evidence, and concluded Kennedy was "probably assassinated as a result of a conspiracy"; a 1982 National Academy of Sciences panel later rejected that acoustic analysis. Persistent public doubt, with polls indicating over 60% rejecting the lone-gunman explanation, stems from withheld documents, witness inconsistencies, and institutional opacity, fueling theories implicating CIA elements opposed to Kennedy's policies, organized crime, or anti-Castro exiles.
